title: The Garden on the Moon
author: Tadoku Note (original)
summary: 月面基地で植物を育てる仕事をしている少年カイ。基地の空気装置が故障したとき、彼の小さな庭が大切な役目を果たします。

source.note: Original text written for this app.

paragraphs: Kai was fourteen years old, and he had never seen rain. He was born on the Moon, in a place called Tranquility Base, about two hundred meters under the gray surface. Two hundred and forty people lived there. They worked in the mines, in the labs and in the control room. Kai’s job, after school, was in the garden.

The garden was the most beautiful place on the base. It was a long room with a white ceiling full of bright lights. There were rows and rows of tomatoes, lettuce, beans and potatoes. There were small trees with lemons on them. The air smelled of earth and leaves. It was the only place on the Moon that smelled alive.

The garden was not just for food. The plants also helped to make the air. They took in carbon dioxide and gave out oxygen. But the main oxygen machines did most of that work. The garden was only a small help. That is what everyone thought.

Kai’s teacher in the garden was an old woman named Dr. Okafor. She had come from Nigeria, on Earth, forty years ago. She talked to the plants. Kai thought that was strange at first. Then he started doing it too.
“Plants are patient,” she told him. “They don’t hurry. They don’t complain. They just do their job, quietly, every day. Remember that, Kai.”

One night, Kai woke up because the lights in his room were flashing red. A calm computer voice was speaking. “Warning. Main oxygen system failure. Please remain calm. Please go to your assigned area.”

Kai’s mother was an engineer. She was already putting on her work clothes. “The main machine has broken down,” she said. “The backup machine is working, but it is old. It can only make enough oxygen for half of the base. We need to fix the main machine, but it will take time.”
“How much time?” asked Kai.
His mother did not answer. That was the worst answer.

In the control room, the base commander explained the problem to everyone. The backup machine would give them about forty-eight hours. The engineers needed at least four days to repair the main machine. A rescue ship from Earth could not arrive for six days.

Then Dr. Okafor stood up. “The garden,” she said. “If we turn the lights on for twenty-four hours a day, the plants will make more oxygen. If we bring every plant from every lab into the garden, and if we use the seeds we have stored, we can make more.”
“How much more?” asked the commander.

Dr. Okafor looked at Kai. Kai had been doing the calculations in his head. He did them every week for his school project. “Not enough to save everyone,” he said slowly. “But enough to give the engineers two or three more days.”
The room was silent. Then the commander said, “Do it.”

For the next five days, Kai hardly slept. With Dr. Okafor and twenty volunteers, he carried trays of plants from every corner of the base. They planted fast-growing seeds in every empty container they could find: old boxes, cut-up water bottles, even helmets. The lights in the garden never went off. The room became hot and wet, like a jungle.

To save oxygen, everyone else on the base had to rest as much as possible. Schools closed. People lay in their beds and moved very little. They talked quietly. Some people played cards. Some read old books. The base was so quiet that Kai could hear the water moving through the pipes.
On the third day, Kai felt dizzy. His head hurt. The oxygen level was getting low. He sat down between two rows of beans and closed his eyes. Dr. Okafor sat next to him.
“Talk to them,” she said, pointing at the plants. “It helps.”
Kai laughed weakly. But he talked. He told the beans about Earth, about rain and oceans and mountains, all the things he had seen only in videos. He told them he wanted to see real rain one day.
On the fifth day, the lights in the base stopped flashing. The computer voice said, “Main oxygen system restored.” Across the whole base, people cheered. Kai heard them through the walls.

Later, the commander came to the garden. She looked at the hot, green jungle and at the boy sleeping between the beans. “The engineers worked fast,” she said to Dr. Okafor. “But they couldn’t have done it without this time. Your garden saved us.”
“Not my garden,” said Dr. Okafor. “His.” And she gently put a blanket over Kai.

A year later, Kai traveled to Earth for the first time, for a science program for young people. On his second day, the sky turned dark, and something cold touched his face. Then another drop, and another.
He stood in the street with his face turned up to the sky, laughing, while everyone around him ran for cover.
